content: The bacteria responsible for gonorrhea have developed resistance to nearly every antibiotic that has been used to treat the infection. It is only a matter of time before resistance emerges to the last remaining effective treatment option. Drug resistance, also known as antimicrobial resistance, occurs when microorganisms such as bacteria or fungi evolve mechanisms to withstand the effects of drugs designed to eliminate them. This means the drugs fail to kill the bacteria, allowing them to continue to grow and spread. Gonorrhea has already become resistant to almost all antibiotics previously used for its treatment. Currently, the only effective class of antibiotics available for treating gonorrhea is cephalosporins. This situation represents a significant public health threat, as the ability to treat gonorrhea effectively is critical for controlling its spread in the United States. Gonorrhea has a remarkable ability to adapt and develop resistance to antibiotics, necessitating ongoing surveillance and the development of new therapeutic options. In the United States, surveillance for drug-resistant gonorrhea is conducted through several initiatives, including the Gonococcal Isolate Surveillance Project (GISP), the enhanced Gonococcal Isolate Surveillance Project (eGISP), and the Strengthening the United States Response to Resistant Gonorrhea (SURRG) program. A key component of these programs is antibiotic susceptibility testing, which determines the effectiveness of antibiotics against gonorrhea. When laboratory testing shows that higher-than-expected concentrations of an antibiotic are required to inhibit bacterial growth, the bacteria are considered to have decreased susceptibility to that antibiotic. The CDC recommends that certain gonorrhea isolates, such as those from infections that fail to respond to recommended treatments or those showing intermediate or full resistance, be submitted to the CDC STD Laboratory for confirmation. Healthcare providers and health departments can report suspected treatment failures or cases of decreased susceptibility to cephalosporins using the Suspected Gonorrhea Treatment Failure Consultation Form. For further inquiries, providers can contact the CDC via email at GCFAILURE@cdc.gov. A significant challenge in monitoring emerging resistance in gonorrhea is the decline in the use of culture-based testing by clinicians and laboratories. Culture testing involves growing bacteria on a nutrient medium and exposing them to antibiotics to assess their susceptibility. However, many clinicians now rely on newer diagnostic technologies, such as Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests (NAATs), which do not allow for antibiotic susceptibility testing. Currently, there is no well-established technology for performing susceptibility testing on non-culture specimens. To address this issue, the CDC recommends that all state and local health department laboratories either maintain or develop the capacity to perform gonorrhea culture testing or establish partnerships with laboratories that can perform these tests. The history of gonorrhea treatment highlights the ongoing challenge of drug resistance. In 1993, the recommended treatments for gonorrhea included ciprofloxacin (a fluoroquinolone) and two cephalosporins (ceftriaxone and cefixime). However, resistance to ciprofloxacin was first detected in Hawaii and the West Coast in the late 1990s and early 2000s. By 2004, ciprofloxacin resistance had become widespread among men who have sex with men (MSM), leading to its discontinuation for this population. By 2006, approximately 14% of gonorrhea samples were resistant to ciprofloxacin, and resistance was observed across all regions of the United States, including among heterosexual individuals. As a result, the CDC stopped recommending fluoroquinolones for gonorrhea treatment in 2007. The cephalosporins, cefixime and ceftriaxone, became the only remaining recommended treatments. However, the CDC has observed concerning trends of decreasing susceptibility to cephalosporins, similar to patterns seen globally. To preserve the effectiveness of cephalosporins, the CDC has frequently updated its STI Treatment Guidelines since 2010. Currently, the first-line treatment for gonorrhea is a single 500 mg dose of the injectable cephalosporin ceftriaxone. The CDC continues to monitor resistance to cephalosporins and other antibiotics. To date, there have been no confirmed reports of clinical treatment failures with cephalosporins in the United States.
